title: What are Compressed Oops?
keyPoints: Compressed Oops (Ordinary Object Pointers) use 4 bytes for references instead of 8 on 64-bit JVMs
Works when heap is < 32 GB – references are shifted left by 3 bits (8-byte alignment)
Saves ~20-30% heap memory compared to uncompressed 64-bit pointers
Enabled by default on 64-bit JVMs with -Xmx < 32g
If heap exceeds 32 GB, compressed oops are disabled and all references use 8 bytes

s1_definition.oneliner: Compressed Oops use 4 bytes for object references on 64-bit JVMs with <32GB heap, saving ~20-30% memory by encoding 35-bit addresses in 32 bits via 8-byte alignment.
s1_definition.profdef:
How it works:

- **64-bit JVM without compression:** Every reference is 8 bytes.
- **With compressed oops:** References are 4 bytes, shifted left by 3 bits (8-byte aligned objects).
- **4 bytes can address 2^32 × 8 = 32 GB** of heap.
- **Savings:** For an object with 10 reference fields, 40 bytes saved (10 × 4 bytes).
s1_definition.analogy: Instead of writing full 8-digit addresses for every bank account, the system uses short 4-digit codes that map to the full address. Works as long as the total number of accounts stays under 32 billion (32 GB).

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  64-bit JVM:
    Without compression: reference = 8 bytes → expensive
    With compression:    reference = 4 bytes → saves ~20-30%
    Works for heap < 32 GB (4 bytes × 8-byte alignment = 32 GB)

  Above 32 GB: compression disabled → all references 8 bytes
  Tip: 31 GB compressed can hold more than 33 GB uncompressed
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Compressed Oops use 4 bytes for references instead of 8 on 64-bit JVMs with heaps under 32 GB. This saves 20-30% heap memory. Above 32 GB, compression is disabled and references double in size. Keep heap under 32 GB when possible.

One sentence to remember: compressed oops halve reference size to 4 bytes – works under 32 GB heap, saves 20-30% memory.
